You know, there have been several studies already from consultants at the city design competitions, the Army Corps of Engineers, who have proposed ways to, to reduce the risk of flooding. But the goal of this effort right now is to get a better handle on how feasible are they, what are the main implications of that so that it can be a solid foundation for large community discussions that are needed about the best way to proceed. So just for those in the audience that aren't familiar, this project does not involve the design or construction of any of these things that we're talking about. Those are things that would come in a future phase. But when we talk about sea level rise, you know, we're not talking about 2100. This was a picture from December. We already have quite a lot of. So for San Rafael, San Rafael is the most vulnerable community in the Bay Area. And it's really a current risk rather than a future risk. So when we think about why San Rafael, the most vulnerable community in the Bay Area, physically, when you think about it, it's so simple story in the sense that the land is very low, that land is also sinking, and what is sort of blocking the water, keeping the water out during the high tides right now is very informal. And so I'll just step through those. And then to add, we have tens of more than 10,000 people living in a very small area. So before the urbanization that happened, San Rafael looked kind of like what China Camp looks like. So there's this ground, and then in between, the wetlands came up into the valleys. So San Rafael, on the hill behind us here in 1901, looked the same. So this is the bank of America building today, and all the way back into Gerstel park, where the tidal channels. So as you develop on top of those areas, it just sort of has an inherent flood risk of building on wetlands and lowlands. In addition, San Rafael, if we were looking out towards, towards the East Bay, this is the point sand. This is where the bridge to Richmond sort of takes up. Originally, the shoreline had this curved shape. Everything that is Target and Home Depot in that area was just wetlands or was part of the bay. So a lot of the southeastern part of the city is actually built on what was the bay. Very thick bay muds or fill. So this is as recently as the 60s. You can still see that sort of natural foundation of the wetland and the fill being placed to enable the development of businesses and homes on top of that. But the way that it was developed was sort of from a low, sort of low elevation and just adding a little bit extra on top of that. And so what we have now is land that's close to the bay, that's just a few inches higher than the bay during that high tide. And the ground is also going down because it's built in on the wetlands and the thick bay muds. Over the past several decades, the ground has been. Has been sinking very slowly, gradually. But as you add those little bits up, it means that some places, like this area by our pump station, the ground's gone down two feet since the 70s, and just because of the soils, is expected to go down another two to four feet in the coming years. So we have those two changes happening at the same time. The ground is going down while the water is coming up. So if one goes down by one foot and the water goes up by one foot, we've got a two foot change there that's, that's creating this amplified risk. And it's not everywhere. Fortunately, much of the areas that are shown in green here are stable. And it's really kind of most pronounced in the areas where we have those thick bay mods, those areas that were built on film. And some of these areas were intentionally designed extra high, knowing that that was going to happen. But that's not the case universally. So all this means that right now, today and this year, we have land that's lower than the bay. And they're a mix of materials, drop boards or planter boxes, they're not in great shape. But all these little private yards and gardens are serving a very public purpose of keeping 101 dry, keeping 580 dry, keeping the wastewater treatment plant dry. And so even though they're sort of small and ad hoc, they're serving a very big purpose for all of us who use those who live here. The other challenge with, with the condition here in San Rafael is that we have a lot of buildings that are half on land and half on water and they're just a few inches above the highest tide. So as this tide goes up another 3, 4 inches or we have a storm, there's a risk that folks homes are affected by the flooding. So along the canal we have a lot of buildings that are in that, that kind of condition. So I'll mention that we're doing a feasibility study, which I mentioned before, with the engineering team and many Folks involved with expertise from New Orleans and the Bay Area. And so they're looking at what are the feasible ways that we can prepare. And that study is ongoing and they're very much in the middle of it. So we're just at the draft phase of trying to fact find. So we're not ready to present on the findings of that, but just to give a preview as we think about the kind of options that are available. Obviously, one option is to not act quickly enough, and everything is kind of in comparison to that baseline scenario. But they're looking at essentially three alternatives. One, to put something between the water and the land, to find a way to raise the shoreline or raise a street, to act as a barrier. Another, to look at a type of barrier that would be in the canal. And then a third strategy of elevating incrementally over time. And all of these strategies, I'll just say we're not talking about them in detail today because all of these strategies involve a level of planning, design, construction that takes at a minimum, several years to decades.
